es: Adaptar un mensaje de viaje al lector británico o estadounidense y usar palabras neutras cuando no conoces su variedad.

teaching.en: Before you write to a British friend, remember that trainers and a jumper are what an American reader would call sneakers and a sweater.
teaching.es: Antes de escribir a un amigo británico, recuerda que «trainers» y «jumper» es lo que un lector estadounidense llamaría «sneakers» y «sweater».
teaching.explanationEs: Trainers y jumper (RU) = sneakers y sweater (EE. UU.).
segments: Before you write to a British friend, remember that trainers and a
jumper are what an American reader would call sneakers and a sweater.
teaching.audioText: Before you write to a British friend, remember that trainers and a jumper are what an American reader would call sneakers and a sweater.

teaching.en: Please put your luggage in the boot of the car, or in the trunk if the driver is American, before we set off for the coast.
teaching.es: Por favor, pon tu equipaje en el «boot» del coche, o en el «trunk» si el conductor es estadounidense, antes de salir hacia la costa.
teaching.explanationEs: Boot (RU) = trunk (EE. UU.): el maletero del coche.
segments: Please put your luggage in the boot of the car, or in the
trunk if the driver is American, before we set off for the coast.
teaching.audioText: Please put your luggage in the boot of the car, or in the trunk if the driver is American, before we set off for the coast.

teaching.en: Take the rubbish out before we leave, and we will stop for petrol on the way; American readers would write trash and gas instead.
teaching.es: Saca la basura antes de salir, y pararemos a echar gasolina por el camino; los lectores estadounidenses escribirían «trash» y «gas».
teaching.explanationEs: Rubbish y petrol (RU) = trash y gas (EE. UU.).
segments: Take the rubbish out before we leave, and we will stop for
petrol on the way; American readers would write trash and gas instead.
teaching.audioText: Take the rubbish out before we leave, and we will stop for petrol on the way; American readers would write trash and gas instead.

teaching.en: A careful writer will adapt the vocabulary to the reader, using sneakers for someone from Boston and trainers for someone from London.
teaching.es: Un escritor cuidadoso adapta el vocabulario al lector: «sneakers» para alguien de Boston y «trainers» para alguien de Londres.
teaching.explanationEs: Adapt to + lector: elegir las palabras que entiende quien lee.
segments: A careful writer will adapt the vocabulary to the reader, using
sneakers for someone from Boston and trainers for someone from London.
teaching.audioText: A careful writer will adapt the vocabulary to the reader, using sneakers for someone from Boston and trainers for someone from London.

teaching.en: If you do not know your audience, choose a neutral word such as car or shoes, or add a short explanation in brackets.
teaching.es: Si no conoces a tu público, elige una palabra neutra como «car» o «shoes», o añade una breve explicación entre paréntesis.
teaching.explanationEs: Neutral = entendible en todas las variedades; audience = las personas que leerán tu texto.
segments: If you do not know your audience, choose a neutral word such
as car or shoes, or add a short explanation in brackets.
teaching.audioText: If you do not know your audience, choose a neutral word such as car or shoes, or add a short explanation in brackets.

teaching.en: For an international reader, steer clear of slang that only locals know, spell out any regional word you cannot replace, and tone down humour that may not travel.
teaching.es: Para un lector internacional, evita la jerga que solo conocen los locales, explica con detalle cualquier palabra regional que no puedas sustituir y rebaja el humor que no se entienda fuera.
teaching.explanationEs: Steer clear of, spell out y tone down son tres maneras de cuidar un mensaje para otros lectores.
segments: For an international reader, steer clear of slang that only locals know, spell out
any regional word you cannot replace, and tone down humour that may not travel.

prompt.es: Elige la versión adaptada por completo para una lectora de Nueva York.

choices.text: Put your trash outside before you leave, then take your sneakers and a jumper out of the boot.
Put your trash outside before you leave, then take your sneakers and a sweater out of the trunk.
Put your rubbish outside before you leave, then take your sneakers and a sweater out of the trunk.

feedback.es: Solo una versión cambia las cuatro palabras británicas: trash, sneakers, sweater y trunk; las demás dejan una.

hint.es: Comprueba que no quede ninguna de las cuatro palabras británicas.

origin.text: Draft for a British reader: 'Put your rubbish outside before you leave, then take your trainers and a jumper out of the boot.'

prompt.es: Completa con la aclaración para EE. UU.: «el maletero».

feedback.es: La aclaración entre paréntesis da el equivalente estadounidense de boot: trunk.

hint.es: Es el equivalente estadounidense de boot que viste en el diálogo.

origin.text: When you do not know where your reader comes from, add a short note in brackets: 'Please put the bags in the boot (___ in the US).'

prompt.es: Ordena: «Si no conoces a tu lector, elige una palabra neutra.»

answer.text: If you do not know your reader choose a neutral word

feedback.es: La condición If you do not know va primero y la recomendación choose a neutral word cierra la frase.

hint.es: Empieza por la condición con If.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada palabra británica con su equivalente estadounidense.

feedback.es: Son cinco pares regulares: cada palabra británica tiene un equivalente distinto en EE. UU.

prompt.es: Escucha el pódcast y elige qué cambio hizo la presentadora tras recibir un mensaje.

choices.text: She stopped giving tips about packing clothes.
She added a list of American words to every episode.
She replaced regional words with neutral ones.

feedback.es: Tras la queja, sustituyó trainers, jumper y boot por shoes, top y car, palabras que entiende todo el mundo.

origin.audio: In my travel podcast I always try to check who is listening. Last month a listener from Canada wrote to say that my tip about packing your trainers and a jumper in the boot of the car had confused half her group. So now I say things like, pack comfortable shoes and a warm top, and leave your bags in the car. Neutral words may sound a little boring, but nobody has to stop and ask.

prompt.es: Reescribe la frase del estímulo para un lector estadounidense.

answer.text: I left my sneakers and my sweater in the trunk.
accepted: I left my sneakers and my sweater in the trunk.
I left my sneakers and sweater in the trunk.
I left my sneakers and my sweater in the car trunk.

feedback.es: Para un lector de EE. UU.: sneakers, sweater y trunk sustituyen a trainers, jumper y boot.

origin.text: I left my trainers and my jumper in the boot.

prompt.es: Escucha el fragmento de la reunión y elige qué decidió el equipo al final.

choices.text: To use neutral words and add a note about regional ones.
To write the whole welcome pack in American English only.
To send two different packs, one per country.

feedback.es: Eligieron palabras neutras y una nota para las regionales; no eligieron una sola variedad ni dos paquetes.

origin.audio: Before we send the welcome pack to our new students, we have to decide whose English to use. Our office is in Manchester, but most of the students are from Texas and Ohio. I suggested using American words such as sneakers and trunk, yet my colleague pointed out that a few of the students come from Dublin, where boot and jumper are perfectly normal. In the end we chose neutral words and added a short note explaining the regional ones.

prompt.es: Escucha otra vez y elige por qué se opone la colega a usar solo palabras americanas.

choices.text: Because American words are harder to learn than British ones.
Because the audience is not made up only of Americans.
Because the office would have to pay for a new pack.

feedback.es: Recuerda que algunos estudiantes vienen de Dublín, donde boot y jumper son normales: el público es mixto.

origin.audio: Before we send the welcome pack to our new students, we have to decide whose English to use. Our office is in Manchester, but most of the students are from Texas and Ohio. I suggested using American words such as sneakers and trunk, yet my colleague pointed out that a few of the students come from Dublin, where boot and jumper are perfectly normal. In the end we chose neutral words and added a short note explaining the regional ones.

prompt.es: Completa con una palabra neutra: «Deja tus bolsas en la parte trasera del coche.»

feedback.es: Car es neutra: la entienden lectores de todas las variedades, a diferencia de boot o trunk.

origin.text: The email was meant for readers from several countries, so the writer avoided regional words. She wrote neither boot nor trunk: 'Please leave your bags in the back of the ___.'

prompt.es: Escribe dos mensajes de viaje, uno para Tom y otro para Mia, adaptando las palabras.

answer.text: Hi Tom, we leave the station at eight on Saturday morning. Please put your luggage in the boot of the car, and bring your trainers and a warm jumper, because it may rain. We will stop for petrol on the way, and before we go please take the rubbish out. I will organise the snacks. If any word sounds strange, just ask me and I will explain it. Cheers, Ana. Hi Mia, we leave the station at eight on Saturday morning. Please put your luggage in the trunk of the car, and bring your sneakers and a warm sweater, because it may rain. We will stop for gas on the way, and before we go please take the trash out. I will organize the snacks. If any word sounds strange, just ask me and I will explain it. Thanks, Ana.
accepted: Hi Tom, we leave the station at eight on Saturday morning. Please put your luggage in the boot of the car, and bring your trainers and a warm jumper, because it may rain. We will stop for petrol on the way, and before we go please take the rubbish out. I will organise the snacks. If any word sounds strange, just ask me and I will explain it. Cheers, Ana. Hi Mia, we leave the station at eight on Saturday morning. Please put your luggage in the trunk of the car, and bring your sneakers and a warm sweater, because it may rain. We will stop for gas on the way, and before we go please take the trash out. I will organize the snacks. If any word sounds strange, just ask me and I will explain it. Thanks, Ana.

Dear Tom, the plan is to leave the station at eight on Saturday morning. Put your luggage in the boot of the car, and bring your trainers and a jumper, as the weather could turn cold. We need to stop for petrol on the way, and please throw away the rubbish before we go. I will organise the snacks. If anything I wrote is unclear, tell me and I will explain it. Cheers, Ana. Dear Mia, the plan is to leave the station at eight on Saturday morning. Put your luggage in the trunk of the car, and bring your sneakers and a sweater, as the weather could turn cold. We need to stop for gas on the way, and please throw away the trash before we go. I will organize the snacks. If anything I wrote is unclear, tell me and I will explain it. Thanks, Ana.

feedback.es: Un buen texto da el mismo mensaje a dos lectores: hora y lugar iguales, palabras británicas para Tom, estadounidenses para Mia y ortografía coherente con cada variedad.

origin.text: Datos: el sábado salen a las 8:00 de la estación; el coche es de Tom; el equipaje va en el maletero; hay que llevar zapatillas de deporte y un jersey; pararán a echar gasolina y hay que sacar la basura; tú organizas los bocadillos. Escribe un mensaje para Tom (británico) y otro para Mia (estadounidense), con el vocabulario y la ortografía de cada uno (organise / organize).

prompt.es: Lee la nota del editor. ¿Qué sugiere sobre el borrador del viaje?

choices.text: That it should be written in a neutral tone with no humour at all.
That it only needs American spelling throughout.
That it is lively but too local for a mixed audience.

feedback.es: Elogia la viveza del borrador y pide suavizar lo demasiado local; no pide eliminar el humor ni cambiar solo la ortografía.

origin.text: Note from a travel editor: 'Your draft is lively, but some phrases will only work in Britain. Tone down the local slang and spell out any word you cannot replace, for example the boot, which is called the trunk in the US.'

prompt.es: Completa: «Conviene explicar con detalle el significado entre paréntesis.»

feedback.es: Spell out significa explicar algo con todo detalle, en este caso el significado de la palabra regional.

origin.text: Whenever you use a word that part of your audience may not know, it is better to ___ out its meaning in brackets, so that nobody has to stop and guess.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Evita la jerga muy local con lectores que no la conocen.»

answer.text: Steer clear of very local slang with readers who do not know it

feedback.es: Steer clear of + sustantivo significa evitar; with readers who do not know it indica ante quién conviene evitarla.
